mcqs.question: A team builds an always-on real-time inference endpoint for a "weekly top picks" email recommendation feature that only needs to be generated once a week. What is the main issue with this design choice?
options: Real-time endpoints are always more accurate than batch jobs, so this is actually the right choice
It optimizes for tail latency the feature doesn't need, incurring unnecessary infrastructure cost and complexity for a use case that could be precomputed on a schedule with a batch job
Batch inference cannot produce recommendations, only real-time inference can
Weekly features must always use online serving for correctness reasons
mcqs.explanation: This is a classic mismatch: online serving is built and priced for millisecond, per-request latency, which a once-a-week email feature never needs — a scheduled batch job would produce identical predictions at a fraction of the operational cost and complexity. Accuracy is a model-quality property independent of serving pattern (A is false), batch inference is routinely used to produce recommendations (C is false), and there's no correctness requirement forcing online serving for weekly-cadence features (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why does a model-serving process load the model into memory once at startup rather than loading it fresh for every incoming request?
options: Loading the model per-request would add significant, unnecessary latency to every single prediction, since model loading is far slower than running a forward pass
Models cannot be loaded more than once without corrupting their weights
Loading once at startup is only a stylistic preference with no performance impact
This pattern only applies to gRPC servers, not REST servers
mcqs.explanation: Model loading (reading weights from disk, initializing the framework) is typically far slower than a single forward pass, so keeping the model resident in memory means each request only pays the cheap inference cost, not the loading cost — this is a core reason serving frameworks are built as long-running processes rather than per-request scripts. Loading a model multiple times doesn't corrupt weights (B is false), the performance impact of reloading per request is significant, not negligible (C is false), and this load-once pattern applies to both REST and gRPC servers equally (D is false).

mcqs.question: A model that works correctly in the development environment fails in production due to a subtly different library version. What does containerizing the model server most directly prevent?
options: It prevents the model from ever needing retraining

It bundles the model weights, serving code, and exact dependency versions into one artifact, so the production environment is guaranteed to match what was tested, eliminating this class of environment-mismatch failure
It automatically fixes bugs in the model's prediction logic
It removes the need for a serving framework like TensorFlow Serving or TorchServe
mcqs.explanation: Containerization's core value is environment reproducibility — packaging exact dependency versions alongside the code means the same container behaves identically wherever it runs, directly preventing the "worked in dev, broke in prod" failure caused by environment drift. It has nothing to do with retraining schedules (A), doesn't fix logic bugs in the model itself (C), and containers typically still run a serving framework inside them rather than replacing the need for one (D is false).

mcqs.question: A team wants to check whether a new fraud-detection model behaves reasonably on real production traffic, but cannot risk it ever making an actual blocking decision yet. Which rollout pattern fits, and why?
options: Canary release, since it immediately routes a small percentage of real decisions to the new model
Shadow deployment, since the new model runs on real traffic and its predictions are logged for comparison, but never returned or acted upon, giving zero user-facing risk
A/B testing, since it's designed specifically for zero-risk evaluation
Full production rollout, since fraud models should always go straight to 100% traffic
mcqs.explanation: Shadow deployment is exactly the pattern for this requirement: the new model sees real traffic and produces real predictions for comparison purposes, but those predictions never affect an actual decision, giving a genuine zero-risk way to validate behavior before any real exposure. A canary release (A) does let the new model affect real decisions for a slice of traffic, which is more risk than allowed here; A/B testing (C) also acts on the new model's outputs for real users, not risk-free; and jumping straight to full rollout (D) for a fraud model is the opposite of a safe rollout practice.

mcqs.question: A new recommendation model shows better offline accuracy on a held-out evaluation set than the current production model. The team wants to confirm it actually improves revenue before fully switching over. What should they run, and why is this different from a canary release?
options: A canary release, which serves the same measurement purpose as an A/B test

An A/B test, which is a measurement exercise designed to reach statistical confidence on a business metric like revenue, distinct from a canary release's purpose of gradually and safely rolling out based on operational health
Neither is necessary, since offline accuracy already confirms the business impact
Shadow deployment alone is sufficient to measure revenue impact, since it logs all predictions
mcqs.explanation: This is precisely the distinction the topic draws: A/B testing exists to answer "is this actually better on the metric that matters" with statistical rigor, whereas a canary release is a rollout risk-mitigation mechanism ramped based on operational health, not a controlled experiment for measuring business impact. Offline accuracy is a proxy metric and doesn't guarantee real-world revenue impact (C is false), and shadow deployment never returns predictions to users, so it can't measure actual user-facing outcomes like revenue (D is false).

mcqs.question: A real-time fraud-scoring system must approve or decline a transaction within 100ms. Which serving pattern is required, and what infrastructure trade-off does it accept?
options: Batch scoring, since fraud transactions can be flagged after the fact during a nightly run
Online serving, since a per-transaction decision is needed within milliseconds; this requires accepting the cost of always-on standby capacity, even during low-traffic periods
Either pattern works identically for this latency requirement
Online serving eliminates the need to pay for any standby infrastructure
mcqs.explanation: A hard 100ms per-transaction latency requirement rules out batch scoring entirely — only online serving can meet it, and the trade-off is accepting the cost of an always-on server ready to respond instantly, unlike a batch job that only consumes compute during its scheduled run. Batch scoring cannot meet a 100ms per-transaction requirement (A is false, it would only catch fraud after the transaction already completed), the two patterns have very different fit for this latency constraint (C is false), and online serving specifically requires paying for standby capacity, not eliminating that cost (D is false).
